title: Grilling Round 2

short.lead: Your round 1 answers are in the decisions log and on #306. Round 2 asks the 13 questions those answers opened. Most are about the agent's name and branches. I checked three facts on this machine. Git's user name here is "ayden". Your GitHub login is "Ajw2003". GitHub holds 21 AjsAgent/ branches and 60 claude/ branches in this repo. The Copy my reply button is still broken in the browser pane (#335), so type your answers, such as "Grilling round 2 answers: 1A 2A 3B".
short.hint: Tap a row to see what it covers.
items: Seventeen answers, logged as "2026-10-18 - Grilling round 1: aj's answers". Deletes are allowed on the agent's own branches and refused on anyone else's; identity becomes settings, with "<name>sAgent" in place of Claude.
Where the agent's name comes from, where it appears, the credit line, the branch prefix, what counts as the agent's own branch, and the old branches.
Snapshot branches piling up, how a feature knows its parent, the archivist on someone else's branch, and docs in repos you don't own.
Three rules the audit found vague, plus the defaults for the label and writing settings.

choices: q1
1. Where does the agent's name come from?
A
The GitHub login, lowercased, plus "sAgent": ajw2003sAgent for you
Matches your example. It needs the GitHub command-line tool to be signed in. If it isn't, the agent name setting blocks until you set it.
B
Git's user name plus "sAgent": aydensAgent on this machine
Works without GitHub, but git names are often a first name and collide between people.
C
Asked once at install and stored as the setting
Nothing is guessed, but a new user's first session stops to ask a question.
In every option the setting can be changed later.
q2
2. Where does the agent's name appear on a commit?
A
As the commit author's name, with the user's own email, and in the credit line
GitHub links the commit to your account and shows ajw2003sAgent as who wrote it, so agent commits stand apart from yours.
B
Only in the credit line; the author stays the user's own git identity
Commits look like yours in every list; only the message says the agent made them.
Today the commit author is your git identity, and the credit line says "Committed by AJ's agent".
q3
3. What does the credit line say?
A
"Committed by ajw2003sAgent" on commits and "Opened by ajw2003sAgent" on pull requests and issues
One name everywhere, taken from the setting.
B
Keep "Committed by AJ's agent" for you, and use "Committed by <name>sAgent" for anyone else
Your commit history stays consistent, but your setting differs from everyone else's default.
The credit check reads the line from the setting, so either works.
q4
4. What prefix do the agent's branches get?
A
The agent name: ajw2003sAgent/<topic>
Branch, author and credit all say the same name.
B
Keep AjsAgent/ as your own prefix setting; for everyone else, build the prefix from the agent name
Nothing is renamed for you, but your prefix differs from everyone else's.
Existing branches are answered in question 6.
q5
5. What makes a branch the agent's own, so deletes are allowed on it?
A
Its name starts with the agent prefix, or with an extra prefix listed in the settings
Simple to check, and old prefixes can be listed. The catch: if a person starts a branch name with the prefix, the agent treats that branch as its own.
B
Its name has the prefix and the plugin recorded creating it
Stricter, but branches made before the restructure, or recorded by a different session, would not count as the agent's.
Round 1 answer 1 allows deletes only on the agent's own branches.
q6
6. What happens to the 21 AjsAgent/ and 60 claude/ branches already on GitHub?
A
Both prefixes go in your settings as extra agent prefixes; nothing is renamed
They stay the agent's own, so its cleanup still works on them. Nothing on GitHub changes.
B
Rename them to the new prefix, one approval per batch
One naming scheme, but open pull requests and links to those branches break.
Issues #181 and #182 already ask about reporting and renaming the claude/ branches.
q7
7. Snapshot branches from autosave will pile up (round 1 answer 12). Who clears them?
A
Each snapshot branch is deleted once its helper's work is merged. The delete is allowed because it is the agent's own branch
No pile-up, and nothing is lost: the work is already merged.
B
They are listed at session start once there are more than 20, and you approve the deletion
You see every deletion, at the cost of one more question.
This follows round 1 answer 1, which allows deletes on the agent's own branches.
q8
8. How does a feature know which bigger feature it belongs to (round 1 answer 9)?
A
Through GitHub's sub-issue link, which this session already uses
One source of truth that you can see on GitHub; the loop reads it.
B
The design loop keeps its own list of parents and children
Works offline, but the list can disagree with the parent links GitHub shows.
#329 sits under #281, and #334 sits under #306, as sub-issues today.
q9
9. The archivist finds a long comment on someone else's branch. Does it move it (round 1 answer 14)?
A
No: it opens an issue naming the comment, since that branch isn't the agent's to change
Consistent with round 1 answer 1: the agent changes only its own branches.
B
Yes, on a new agent branch cut from theirs, with a pull request
The move still happens, but a pull request lands on someone else's work unasked.
On the agent's own branch the archivist moves it at turn end, as decided.
10. In a repo you don't own, do the six-tier docs get committed?
A
No: they stay local and out of git, unless the owner asks for them
The context layer still works on your machine, and nobody else's repo gets docs it didn't ask for.
B
Yes, on an agent branch with a pull request
The owner gets the docs, but as an unasked pull request.
The two rules conflict. docs-tiers.md:47-48 keeps these docs out of git, while artifact-location.md:6-7 says they are tracked and committable.
11. What counts as a wholesale rewrite, which needs your approval by name?
A
Replacing more than half of a file's lines in one change, or writing the whole file over
A number a check can count, so it is enforced the same way every time.
B
Whatever the agent judges a rewrite to be
Flexible, but two sessions will judge it differently.
edit-place.md:15 uses the word "wholesale" without defining it.
12. When may the agent skip a check because it is too expensive to run?
A
Only when it takes over 10 minutes, costs money, or needs a machine or account the agent can't reach; the reply names which
A plain test, so the end-of-reply check can hold the reply to it.
B
Never: every check runs, however long
Nothing is skipped, but a long test suite delays every turn.
evidence-before-claims.md:38-39 says "not prohibitively expensive" with no threshold.
13. What defaults do the other settings carry?
A
Labels: "<name> created this", "in progress", "needs review". Voice: on. Page threshold: 160 words. None of them block
Someone new gets a working setup with no questions; only the agent name can block (question 1).
B
Every setting blocks until it is set
Nothing is assumed, but a new install asks several questions before it does anything.
Round 1 answer 16: each setting carries a default or blocks until set.
